name: Cherry
summary: Sweet cherry is almost never grown in the Philippines: it needs a long cold winter, so only a few hobbyists in the coolest highland towns such as Baguio and Benguet keep potted trees, which rarely fruit. Farmers who want a cherry like fruit here grow aratiles or acerola, which bear easily in the lowlands. This short guide covers the few highland attempts.
season: Trees are set out at the start of the rains, about May to July, in the highlands. Without enough cold, flowering is weak and irregular.
material: Grafted trees of low chill cherry types from a specialty nursery, kept in big pots or planted on the coolest high ground. Trees from seed seldom bear.
spacing: About 4 to 5 m between trees, or one to a large pot.
water: Rain fed, with watering in dry spells. Never in standing water.
fertilizer: Compost, rotted manure and small amounts of complete fertilizer (14 14 14).
care: Light pruning, steady feeding, netting against birds.
harvest: The few fruits are picked by hand with their stalks when fully colored.

ways.label: Grafted trees (grafted na punla)

steps.title: Choose the coolest spot
steps.how: Pick the highest, coolest sunny ground, with fast drainage, or a large pot of loose soil and compost.

steps.title: Plant at the start of the rains
steps.how: Set the grafted tree at the same depth, graft joint above the soil, about 4 to 5 m apart. Firm, water, stake and mulch.

steps.title: Feed and prune lightly
steps.how: Give compost and a little complete fertilizer (14 14 14) every few months, and keep a few wide branches so light gets in.

steps.title: Pick any ripe fruit
steps.how: We count the first crop at about 48 months. Pick cherries with their stalks when fully colored, and net the tree against birds.

ways.note: We count the first harvest at about 48 months (1,440 days). Most trees here never bear well.

mistakes: Buying imported cherry trees for the lowlands, where they will not fruit.
Confusing sweet cherry with aratiles or acerola, which are different plants.
better: For a sure crop, plant aratiles or acerola, which bear in the lowlands.
If you try sweet cherry, use only low chill types in cool highlands and keep notes.
Test the soil and feed by the result.

watering.traditional: The rare cherry trees here grow in big pots or on the coolest high ground and live on rain, with a pail of water in dry spells.
watering.method: A pail or hose into a ring basin, or a watering can for pots, in the morning.
watering.rainfed: Plant as the rains begin on the coolest sunny ground with fast drainage, or in a big pot of loose soil and compost. In the ground, rain carries the tree with a pail of water in dry spells.
watering.dryseason: Trees in the ground when the soil a hand deep is dry. Trees in pots every day or two in dry, sunny weather.
watering.wet: Cherry roots rot in wet soil: never plant where water stands, and make sure pots drain freely.

schedule.often: Soak at planting, then whenever the soil dries in a dry spell, until the tree is clearly growing
schedule.amount: A good soak of the mulched ring around the stem
schedule.why: The roots are still in the bag ball and the tree is not yet established.

schedule.often: Only in dry spells, when the soil a hand deep is dry
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the ring, never leaving water standing
schedule.why: These trees grow in cool, wet uplands, where rain usually covers them.

schedule.stage: Flowering to four weeks after bloom (in a year it flowers)
schedule.often: Never let the soil dry out
schedule.amount: A deep soak whenever the soil a hand deep is dry. A pot every day or two
schedule.why: Stress now cuts fruit set and size.

schedule.stage: Final swell, the last three weeks before picking
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the ring
schedule.why: Cherries gain most of their size in the last three weeks.

critical: Flowering to about four weeks after bloom.
The last three weeks before picking.

signs.dry: Leaves droop and brown at the edges, and fruits drop or stay small.
signs.wet: Yellow leaves and dying roots in soggy soil or a pot that does not drain.

better: Keep the soil steadily moist at flowering and in the last three weeks before picking.
